In the year 1000, the most powerful man in Baghdad was not the caliph.

This map of West and South Asia shows a world of Turkic warlords, Shia dynasties and Christian kingdoms on the Nile — almost none of which survive.

a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ Start with the Buyids, the teal block over Iraq and western Iran. They were Shia Iranians who took Baghdad in 945 and kept the Sunni Abbasid caliph on as a figurehead — the spiritual head of Sunni Islam, ruled by men who did not share his sect.

2/ To the east, the Ghaznavid Empire. Its founders were Turkic slave-soldiers who had served the Samanids and then outgrew them. Under Mahmud of Ghazni (998–1030) it ran from Iran into the Punjab, funded heavily by campaigns into northern India.

3/ The Karakhanid Khanate, top right, is easy to skip and shouldn't be. They were the first major Turkic dynasty to adopt Islam — the start of a shift that made Central Asia Muslim and Turkic rather than Buddhist and Iranian.

4/ Khotan was that older world: a Buddhist oasis kingdom on the Silk Road, famous for jade and for its own Iranian language. The Karakhanids took it around 1006. Its manuscripts survive in museums; its kingdom does not.

5/ Now look at Arabia. The 'Qarmatian Republic' on the Gulf coast was a radical Ismaili state that sacked Mecca in 930 and carried off the Black Stone of the Kaaba, holding it for roughly two decades before it was returned.

6/ And the strangest survivors: Makuria and Alodia, in green along the Nile. Christian Nubian kingdoms in what is now Sudan, they had held off Arab armies for centuries under a negotiated truce. Makuria lasted into the 1300s.

7/ Of everything labelled on this map, only Oman is still a state under the same name. A map of the world's great powers has a shelf life of a few centuries at most.
